title: Where things are
intro: This unit adds the first case ending, the locative `-DA`, and the two words Turkish uses for existence, *var* and *yok*. You'll also see how suffixes attach to names, after an apostrophe, and why **on it** is *onda*, with an extra n.

blocks.text: Turkish has no prepositions like **in**, **at** or **on**. A suffix on the noun does the job: *ev* (house) → *evde* (at home, in the house). This suffix, the locative (*bulunma hâli*), is `-DA`: it follows two-way harmony, *-de* or *-da*, and its d can turn into t, as the next section shows.
One suffix covers all three English prepositions, and the context tells you which: *masada* is on the table, *çantada* in the bag, *kapıda* at the door.

To say where someone **is**, add the personal endings of **to be** after `-DA`. Since `-DA` ends in a vowel, the buffer *y* appears before `-Im` and `-Iz`: *evdeyim*, *evdeyiz*. The negative and the question work as in [unit 4](a1-u04): *evde değilim*, *evde misin?*

rows.en: he, she or it is at home
you are at home (plural or polite)

items.en: The book is on the table.

blocks.text: French uses à, dans and sur where Turkish has one ending: à la maison → *evde*, dans le sac → *çantada*, sur la table → *masada*.
The locative says where something **is**, not where it goes. **I'm going home** needs a different ending, the dative `-(y)A` of [unit 7](gp-dative).

A suffix that starts with d changes it to t after a voiceless consonant: f, s, t, k, ç, ş, h, p. Turkish schoolchildren remember them as *fıstıkçı şahap* (Şahap the pistachio seller), a phrase made of exactly these letters. After a vowel or any other consonant, the d stays d.

lines: -DA → -ta / -te   after f, s, t, k, ç, ş, h, p

items.en: The children are in the park.
The book isn't in the bag, it's in the kitchen.
Is the teacher in the classroom?

blocks.text: The stem itself doesn't change: *kitapta*, *sokakta*, with the p and k kept. The same change happens to every suffix that starts with D, such as the formal `-DIr` of [unit 3](gp-copula-present): *kitaptır*, *Türk'tür*. It doesn't touch *dA* (too), which is a separate word: *kitap da*.
Assimilation follows the last **sound**, not the last letter. Foreign names take the suffix their pronunciation calls for: *Paris'te*, but *Bordeaux'da*, because the name ends in an o sound.

sections.title: There is, there isn't: var and yok

blocks.text: *Var* means **there is** or **there are**, and *yok* means **there isn't** or **there aren't**. They come at the end of the sentence, usually after a place in the locative: place, then the thing, then *var* or *yok*.

items.en: There's a book on the table.
There are children in the park.
Isn't there anybody in the café?

blocks.text: Questions add `mI` as usual: *var mı?* (is there?), *yok mu?* (isn't there?). The short answers are *Evet, var* and *Hayır, yok*; in casual speech *Var* or *Yok* alone is enough.
*Kimse* means **anybody**, and with *yok* **nobody**: *Evde kimse yok* (There's nobody at home). It also works in questions: *Kafede kimse var mı?* (Is there anybody in the café?).

**New or known?** Use *var* to introduce something new, often with *bir*: *Masada bir kitap var* (There's a book on the table). For something the listener already knows about, put the locative on the place and use **to be**: *Kitap masada* (The book is on the table). The first answers **what is there?**, the second **where is it?**
*Yok* is the opposite of *var*, not of **is**. *Ali evde değil* (Ali isn't at home) says where Ali isn't; *Evde kimse yok* (There's nobody at home) says the house is empty.
*Var* and *yok* also give Turkish its way of saying **have**: *Arabam var* (I have a car, literally my car exists). That comes in [unit 9](gp-possessive-have).

When a suffix goes on a proper noun, the name of a person, a city, a country or a river, an apostrophe (*kesme işareti*) separates it from the name: *İstanbul'da*, *Ayşe'de*, *Türkiye'de*. Common nouns take none: *evde*, *şehirde*. The suffix still follows harmony and assimilation as usual.

Numbers written in digits and abbreviations take an apostrophe too, and the suffix follows the way they are **read**: *2026'da* (in 2026, read *iki bin yirmi altıda*), *1453'te* (read *bin dört yüz elli üçte*, ending in ç), *TDK'de* (read *te de ke*).

items.note: literally, the key is at Ayşe

blocks.text: No apostrophe goes on common nouns, on words built from a name with a suffix that makes a new word (*İstanbullu*, from Istanbul; *Türkçe*, Turkish), or on the names of institutions and organizations (*Türk Dil Kurumunda*, at the Turkish Language Association). You met the apostrophe with nationalities in [unit 3](gp-copula-present): *Türk'üm*, but *Kanadalıyım*.
Without the apostrophe, *İstanbulda* is still understood, but it is a spelling mistake. And never add one to a common noun: *şehirde*, not *şehir'de*.

sections.title: Onda, burada: pronouns and place words

blocks.text: The demonstratives *bu*, *şu* and *o* add an n before a case ending: *bunda* (in this, on this), *şunda* (in that), *onda* (in it, on him or her). Their plurals don't: *bunlarda*, *onlarda*. The personal pronouns don't either: *bende*, *sende*, *bizde*, *sizde*.

head: Word
+ locative
Meaning
rows: in it; on him or her

blocks.text: With people, the locative often means **has it on them**: *Anahtar bende* (I've got the key), *Kalem onda* (She has the pen). You'll see this again with *kimde?* (who has it?) in [unit 10](gp-whose).
The place words are the locative of stems that never stand alone in this form: *bura-* (this place), *şura-* (that place), *ora-* (that place over there) and *nere-* (what place).

head: Word
Meaning
rows: there, right there (near you, or where I'm pointing)

items.en: The book is over there, on the table.

blocks.text: *Onda* (on it, he has it) and *oda* (room) are different words: the n matters. And *bende* (on me) is one word, while *ben de* (me too) is two ([unit 4](gp-de-also)).
In speech you'll hear *burda*, *şurda*, *orda* and *nerde*. In writing, use the full forms: *burada*, *şurada*, *orada*, *nerede*.

summary: The locative `-DA` means in, at or on, and takes the endings of **to be**: *evdeyim*, *evde değilim*, *evde misin?*
`-DA` becomes *-ta* or *-te* after f, s, t, k, ç, ş, h, p (*fıstıkçı şahap*): *parkta*, *ofiste*.
*Var* (there is) and *yok* (there isn't) end the sentence: *Masada bir kitap var.* *Evde kimse yok.*
Something new: *var*. Something known: locative + **to be**: *Kitap masada.*
Names, numbers and abbreviations keep an apostrophe before the suffix: *İstanbul'da*, *Ayşe'de*, *2026'da*.
*Bu*, *şu*, *o* add n before a case ending: *bunda*, *onda*. The place words are *burada*, *şurada*, *orada*, *nerede*.
